newsitem.title: USA: Greenspan Q&A, PART II - Productivity, CPI bias.
newsitem.headline: Greenspan Q&A, PART II - Productivity, CPI bias.

text.p: The following are excerpts from the question-and-answer session following the first leg of Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan's semi-annual Humphrey-Hawkins address before Congress.
Greenspan addressed the Senate Banking Committee at 1000 EST/1500 GMT.

SEN. SHELBY (R-Ala.): "We see a big rise in the stock market, but a great proportion of that money is not held by the individual stockholders. It's the pension funds and institutional invenstors (who) have benefitted. When we see the market go up as much as it has, does it necessarily mean that individuals are benefitting?"

GREENSPAN: "Remember that everyone's 401Ks have got some of that, and then there are still these very large defined contribution benefit programs which hold a majority of equities in their accounts. If one were to take the total market value of stocks and ... try to allocate what's in pension funds and life insurance or whatever, a significant part would end up as increased assets net in the lower-income groups."
SEN. SHELBY: "How does the Federal Reserve reconcile the apparent shortcomings in productivy measurements?"

GREENSPAN: "We suspect that our productivty measures in the manufacturing area are probably not too bad. Even though we do have some difficulty measuring output of goods, we probably come as close as you can get in getting right numbers in manufacturing output.

"We have a very difficult time in measuring output and therefore productivity in a vast number of services. Clearly in the medical services profession, in the legal profession, in business services generally.

"... The last 20 years, for a lot of major service industries, the level of productivity (as measured by the Commerce Department in constructing national income and product accounts) has been going down by 1.0 to 2.0 percent a year, which is clearly just utterly non-credible considering the technologies we are all aware of in medical services and the legal area.
SEN. SHELBY: "But is the measurement of productivity a key issue in measuring inflation?"

GREENSPAN: "Yes, it is because to the extent that we have only dollar information on output and we must convert those dollars into real units, the price indexes employed to do that are obviously very crucial.

"If, as is almost surely the case, there is significant upward bias especially in these service areas, you get a situation in which the measure of productivity very evidently is bias as indeed the price indexes are biased.

"The fact that the productivity data are so non-credible suggests the prices are biased. That's one of the reasons we believe the Boskin Commission's estimate of CPI price bias, from where we can judge it, is probably fairly accurate."
